lesson.title: Terror in Response to Freedom: The Origins of the Ku Klux Klan
lesson.summary: Founded by Confederate veterans in Tennessee at the end of 1865, the Ku Klux Klan grew within a few years into an organized campaign of racial terrorism aimed at destroying Black political power and reversing the gains of Radical Reconstruction.
lesson.body:
In the winter of 1865 and 1866, a group of former Confederate veterans in Pulaski, Tennessee, founded a private social club they called the Ku Klux Klan, adopting hooded costumes and secret rituals that at first seem to have been intended more for entertainment and camaraderie than for organized violence. That character changed quickly. As Black Southerners began exercising new rights under Reconstruction, especially after the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments extended citizenship and the vote, the Klan transformed into something far more dangerous: a paramilitary movement dedicated to destroying Black political and economic independence through terror.

The Klan spread rapidly across the South as a loose network of local chapters, or dens, that operated with little central coordination but a shared purpose. Around 1867, Nathan Bedford Forrest, a former Confederate cavalry general and prewar slave trader with a wartime record already tied to accusations of a massacre of Black Union soldiers at Fort Pillow, emerged as the Klan's first Grand Wizard, giving the loosely organized movement a recognizable, if largely symbolic, national leader.

Klan violence followed a clear pattern aimed at reversing the very gains Radical Reconstruction had made possible. Riders operating at night whipped, beat, and murdered Black political organizers, teachers who ran freedpeople's schools, ministers, and Black business owners who had achieved any measure of independence, along with the white Republican officials and scalawags who supported them. The goal was to terrorize Black communities away from voting, away from asserting legal rights, and away from any economic activity that threatened white control over labor, essentially enforcing through violence the same racial hierarchy that the Black Codes had tried, and largely failed, to enforce through law.

The federal government eventually pushed back. Congress passed a series of Enforcement Acts between 1870 and 1871, including a law commonly called the Ku Klux Klan Act, which made interfering with citizens' voting rights a federal crime and gave President Grant authority to use federal troops and suspend habeas corpus to break up Klan activity. Grant used that power in October 1871, suspending habeas corpus in nine counties in South Carolina where Klan violence was especially severe, and federal prosecutors brought hundreds of cases against Klan members across the South. Forrest himself reportedly called for the Klan to disband around 1869, apparently uneasy with how far the violence had spiraled beyond his control, though local dens continued acting on their own regardless of any formal order.

Federal pressure significantly weakened the original Klan by the mid 1870s, but it did not end racial terrorism in the South. Similar paramilitary groups, including the White League in Louisiana and the Red Shirts in Mississippi and South Carolina, soon took up the same campaign of violence and intimidation against Black voters and Republican governments, carrying the fight into the very years when federal commitment to Reconstruction was beginning to collapse.
